passage: Tuesday, 9:40 pm. Ran the vendor meeting today and, for once, did not let it end with "okay, let's see." Last month we talked for an hour about delivery delays and left with nothing. This time, five minutes before the end, I read out what we had decided: Yogesh will call the courier and get a written delivery date by Thursday; I will send the revised order to the vendor by Friday; we check both in Monday's ten-minute stand-up. I felt a bit pushy saying dates aloud, but nobody objected. Before dinner I typed the three lines into an email and sent it to everyone. Yogesh replied within minutes: "Got it. Thursday." Small thing, but it feels like the meeting finally counted. - Chinmay

qa.q: By when will Yogesh get a written delivery date from the courier?
qa.a: Yogesh will get a written delivery date by Thursday.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel about reading the dates aloud?
qa.a: A bit pushy and self-conscious, though relieved when nobody objected.

qa.q: Why was sending the three lines by email a good step?
qa.a: It put the decisions, owners and dates in writing, so nobody had to rely on memory.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen the closing summary?
qa.a: Yogesh probably found it clear and useful, since the reply "Got it. Thursday." came within minutes.

grounding: Shows a meeting leader closing with each decision, owner and date and sending it in writing.

For three years, the women's group of Chandpur had "decided" on a food stall at the Dussehra fair, and for three years nobody had actually booked a space.
This year Rashmi was running the meeting. They met under the neem tree after the evening milking, and talked for an hour about what to cook: pakoras, jalebis, or both. Then Rashmi held up the group register.
"So, what we decided. Pakoras only. Jasleen, you'll go to the fair office and book the space by Thursday. Kamla tai, you'll buy the besan and oil by the Monday before the fair. I'll borrow the big kadhai from the school by Saturday. Everyone agree?"
Heads nodded. She wrote it down, name by name, date by date, and read it aloud once more. That night she sent a voice note with the same list to everyone's phone.
On Thursday afternoon Jasleen sent a photo of the booking receipt.

qa.q: Who was going to book the space, and by when?
qa.a: Jasleen would go to the fair office and book the space by Thursday.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt reading the list aloud, knowing the last three years?
qa.a: Rashmi probably felt determined and a little hopeful that this time the stall would really happen.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do at the end that other meeting leaders could copy?
qa.a: Rashmi stated each decision with a name and a date, wrote it in the register, read it aloud and sent it as a voice note.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the voice note that night?
qa.a: Jasleen would probably find it a clear, friendly reminder that the booking was Jasleen's to do and by when.

grounding: Shows a meeting leader who closes by naming each decision, owner and deadline and sends it in writing, so the plan actually happens.

passage:
The community garden in Kraków had held the same meeting about the broken fence four times since spring. Each time people agreed it should be fixed. Each time nothing happened.
Olga, who had taken over as coordinator in August, let the talk run for half an hour. Then she stood and read from her notebook. "So we decided: new fence along the north side. Rosa buys the wire by next Friday. Tomasz borrows his brother's post-hole digger for Saturday the twelfth. Marek and I build it that day, from nine. Anyone who can't do their part, tell me by Wednesday."
Rosa laughed. "You're writing it down?"
"And sending it tonight," Olga said.
The email came at nine that evening, three lines long. Rosa printed it and stuck it on her fridge. On Saturday the twelfth, the fence went up by two o'clock, and nobody mentioned it at the next meeting.

qa.q: How many times had the garden held the same meeting about the fence?
qa.a: They had held it four times since spring.

qa.q: What does Rosa's laugh at the notebook suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Rosa seemed surprised and a little amused, since nobody had ever written the decisions down before.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Olga named each task, owner and date, asked people to speak up by Wednesday and emailed it that night, so the fence finally got built.

qa.q: If you were Tomasz, what would the email help you with?
qa.a: It would remind Tomasz exactly what to borrow and for which Saturday, so nothing depended on memory.

grounding: Illustrates a leader who closes a meeting with decisions, owners and dates and sends them in writing, ending a cycle of repeated meetings.

At the end of the staff meeting in the school library, Dolma closed her laptop and stood. The Sports Day discussion had gone round for forty minutes, the same way it had gone last term, when the meeting had had to be held three times.
"Before anyone leaves," Dolma said, "let me read back what we've agreed. Tarun sir books the ground with the municipal office by the fifteenth. Mrs Pillai collects house-wise lists from class teachers by the twentieth. I send the parents' circular by the twenty-second. The next check-in is on the twenty-third, fifteen minutes, only if something is stuck."
Tarun looked up. "Can I have till the eighteenth? The office is closed on Monday."
"Eighteenth," Dolma said, and changed it.
Within an hour the list was in everyone's inbox. On the twenty-third, nobody needed the check-in.

qa.q: By when does Mrs Pillai collect the house-wise lists?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai collects them by the twentieth.

qa.q: Why did Tarun ask for a later date?
qa.a: Tarun was worried about being able to meet the deadline, because the office is closed on Monday, and he wanted an honest date.

qa.q: What made Dolma's ending different from last term?
qa.a: Dolma read back each decision with an owner and a date, adjusted a date when asked, and emailed the list within an hour.

qa.q: How might the other teachers feel on the twenty-third?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and pleased that the extra meeting was not needed.

grounding: Shows a meeting leader who closes by stating decisions, owners and dates and sends them in writing, so no repeat meeting is needed.

Subject: Nani's 80th: who's doing what (please read)
Hi all,
Thanks for staying on the call past eleven. Before we forget it all like last year's anniversary plan (three calls, zero bookings), here is what we decided:
1. Venue: the community hall in Aundh, lunch on Saturday 14 June. Yash books it and sends the receipt to the group by Friday 23rd.
2. Guest list: Priti and I merge our lists into one sheet by Sunday 25th. Everyone adds missing names by Wednesday 28th.
3. Food: Mami calls the caterer from Mitali's wedding and gets two menus by Friday 30th.
4. Photo slideshow: Neel collects old photos from everyone until 5 June.
5. Gift for Nani: we decide on the next call, Sunday 1 June, 8 pm. I'll send the link.
If I've got anything wrong, reply today, not on the 13th of June.
Jatin

qa.q: Who is booking the community hall, and by when?
qa.a: Yash books it and sends the receipt by Friday 23rd.

qa.q: What does "reply today, not on the 13th of June" suggest about Jatin's feelings?
qa.a: Jatin is determined and a little worried, not wanting a repeat of last year's plan that fell apart, so any mistake has to surface early.

qa.q: Why does this email make last year's failure less likely?
qa.a: Every decision has a named owner and a date, and it is written down for everyone, so nothing depends on memory or goodwill.

qa.q: How might Yash feel seeing a name and a date beside the venue?
qa.a: Yash knows exactly what is expected and when, which may feel a little pressured but also clear, with no confusion about who is booking.

grounding: Illustrates a leader who closes a planning call by writing down each decision with an owner and a date and sending it to everyone.
